utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. All the accused are present. Defence teams are full -- full house today; full force, too. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Thayer, Mr. Elderkin. Before we get the witness in, yesterday we heard your submissions, your very learned and constructive, I must say, submissions on the Prosecution fourth motion for leave to amend 65 ter exhibit list, which we have given due consideration to in our deliberations. And as indicated yesterday, we will handing down our decision on this first, and I think then on the remaining two documents from the list of documents that the Prosecution sought to tender in relation to Witness 145 and the two documents that the Gvero Defence team also sought to tender, we postponed our decision until later. So our decision is as follows: First of all, we wish to state that we are guided by our previous decisions on the way such motions should be handled, dealt with. We also wish to enjoin you to exercise the utmost diligence. This will apply not only to the Prosecution, but also to the Defence, because ultimately your case will come up and you will encounter, experience shows you will encounter, the same problem. We will enjoin you all to exercise the utmost diligence and to resort to such motions only when this is essential for a proper administration of justice. We have considered the various submissions. We come to the conclusion that in as far as the one-page montage of four photos obtained from PW-105, PW-105 with unidentified caretakers close to the time of the individual's discharge, no cause has been -- no good cause has been shown, and therefore we are not granting the Prosecution motion for that document to be included in the 65 ter document list. As regards the document being a wound photographs, wound photographs, for the time being we are coming to the conclusion that what is put forward as a good cause by the Prosecution may, at the end of the day, not be proven right. So we are, for the time being, saying that at present no good cause has been shown and therefore the permission to include this -- these photos in -- in the 65 ter list is being withheld, pending further deliberation and determination of the same request, if in the course of cross-examination of that particular witness the need for use of these photographs becomes obvious and evident. The rest -- as regards the rest of the documents related to both Witness 105 and the intercepts related to Witness PW-145, the Trial Chamber is of -- comes to the conclusion that sufficient good cause has been shown and therefore Prosecution is being given authorisation to include them in the 65 ter list. We come now to the two Prosecution lists, two Prosecution documents; namely, the one behind tab 2 and the one behind tab 3. That is English ERN 0320-1098, being an intercept dated 19th [sic] July, and the second one 0320-1099 being also an intercept dated 12th [sic] July; and also the one at tab 10, namely, ERN number 0320-1130. These are being all marked for identification purposes. And as regards the intercepts behind tab 2 and 3, the first two, this decision is being taken after -- also after due consideration of the additional submission by the Gvero Defence team. Then there is six transcripts from tapes TOO 6580, extract 535 and transcript from the same tape, extract 536, these being 65 ter numbers 6D14 and 6D15 respectively. Again, these two are being entered into the records and marked for identification purposes pending the final decision on transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As regards -- to complete the picture, as regards the two documents behind tab 2 and tab 3 to which I referred earlier on, the exception, the plea, or the objection raised by the Gvero Defence team had, at its basis, an allegation that they are not a faithful reflection of the original intercept. This is a matter that will ultimately be reserved to our final deliberation stage. So for that particular reason that for the time being these are entered and marked for identification purposes. All right. I think we can safely proceed with the witness. Yes, Mr. Thayer, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I just want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You could avoid standing behind --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just wanted to make one correction for the record at page 3, line 3, there is a reference to tab 2, the first intercept, being the 19th of July and that in fact is the 11th of July. I know things are confusing enough, and I just wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hadn't noticed that because I wasn't watching everything at the same time, but I thank you for that correction. So, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good morning. Just a brief point. Mr. Stojanovic and I spoke this morning about a point he was making in cross-examination, and we thought it would be helpful to offer you a stipulation and we can bring it in writing. But that is on the intercept 1158A and B, which is a 14 July intercept at 0910 hours. There is a mention of a MUP person named Mane, you may recall the cross-examination. It's -- it is our stipulation that that is not Mane that you may recall from the film, whose name is actually Mendeljejev Djuric from the MUP, and it's the Prosecution's position that that is Mane Djuric, the deputy commander in the CSB Zvornik. Mr. Stojanovic, I believe he agrees with me on that point, and we can put this in writing if you like. These will be important points as we get down the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think you can follow that path. At the same time, please do take into account that it would be a bilateral sort of stipulation with Mr. Stojanovic, not with the others, so perhaps other Defence teams may rally and agree to that stipulation as well. But it's not an invitation, it's just thinking aloud that I am doing that for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Dr. Clark. Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will try to get going straight away. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Clark. Yesterday, I took you through some basic background about your profession and your work in Bosnia. And I'd like to ask just a few more questions now, starting with asking, do you recall testifying here in the Krstic trial?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And prior to that trial, you prepared a report on the work done in the 1998 season. Have you subsequently prepared any further reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a 1999 season that I based on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since then I have produced reports for 2000 and 2001 seasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, briefly what were the findings of those reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- I'm not sure what kind of detail you want them, but they were --

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: A very general overview in terms of the general nature of the persons found in those graves that were examined in those seasons?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a lot of similarities to the cases presented in the Krstic trial. These were all men of wide age range; some with disabilities, a number had blindfolds and ligatures on them. The vast majority had been -- died as a result of gunshot injuries. And like in the other cases, a number we -- in a number of cases, we were unable to come to a conclusion of the cause of death and we had to leave that as unascertained. In one specific site, in Glogova, we found a considerable number of men who had died as a result of blast injuries, so from an explosion rather than bullets; but really apart from that, there was a good similarity in the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And looking at the group --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Elderkin. Just for the record, present in the courtroom during the testimony of Dr. Clark is Dr. Dunjic, who is forensic expert assigned to -- of the Defence teams. Yes, sorry for the interruption. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Looking at the overall group of victims, did you come to any findings as to whether they could have been killed in combat?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depends what you define as combat. If you are suggesting that this was a fully equipped army of fighting men, men of fighting age, with military uniforms and weapons, no there was no evidence of that whatsoever. We found no -- no men with any military clothing at all. None of them had any weapons and only occasionally we found some bullets with the bodies in pockets. I suspect you're not really suggesting that, however. If you are taking it down a stage and suggesting that these were a group of men of fighting age, not a formed army, who did have weapons, well, I can't completely exclude that. Because a substantial number were of what we so call fighting age and could have had weapons and could have been killed in a conflict. However, you have to take into account that a large number of men did not fall into that category. We had young men; particularly, we had a lot of elderly people. We had a number who had physical disabilities, which would prevent them from being able to be effectively in a fighting situation. We also have to take into account that in three graves, at least, there were substantial numbers of men with blindfolds and ligatures. That was particularly in Kozluk and Lazete; and to a lesser extent in the Glogova grave, there were 12 men there were ligatures. So that goes against a fighting unit. Thirdly, I think you've got to take into account that, as much as we could determine, most of the -- the majority of shots killing these men came from behind, which is not perhaps what you would expect in a face-to-face conflict situation. And a substantial number of men were killed by a single shot to the back of the head. And I think the fourth consideration is that in any conflict you will get a lot of wounded men, not all men will be killed. There will be substantial numbers, and arguably more people wounded than killed. We had -- with the occasional exception, there was no evidence of large numbers of people who had been wounded before they died; people with bandaged wounds or any other signs of previous injuries. So really for all these reasons I felt, while I cannot completely exclude that there may have been some conflict situation to some extent, that an awful lot of men could not be accounted for in that way, a lot of the deaths could not be accounted for in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Lastly, I just -- I notice that you've brought with you some papers today. Could you tell us briefly what those are?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are, first of all, my three reports from the seasons, the overall chief pathologist report from 1999, 2000, 2001. I have also the sort of working papers, which I used. I had all the post-mortem reports compiled by all the pathologists, and I went through them and extracted relevant information, which I've put on various working sheets which I then, from them, used to make up the final reports. So that's the bulk of the paperwork I have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. If during any further questioning you need to refer to any of those papers, please do so, and please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, just in relation to your evidence yesterday about the priority in terms of the role of the forensic pathologist being to ascertain the cause of death, what were the limitations that you found in regards your work in those autopsies because many of the remains were skeletal?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are a lot of limitations, and I've set them out in the report. The main problem, these were bodies which had been dead for some considerable time. The tissues had decomposed and a large number were reduced to skeletons. As pathologists, when we are looking at why people have died, we generally are looking at the sort tissues on the body, the skin, and other materials beneath, looking for bruising and swelling and other injuries. That, of course, was virtually absent in a lot of these cases, so we were reduced to our interpretation of any injuries to them as to the damage to the skeleton. The skeleton will of course have remained. So when we are looking for injuries, primarily, we're looking at injuries in the skeleton. Now -- so that was one thing. The -- trying to say whether an injury to a skeleton, to a bone, occurred before death or just after death is actually very difficult, if not at some stage impossible. Because the bone, you will only see evidence that it's occurred in life once the healing process starts in a bone and that usually takes at least a number of days. So, theoretically, all the injuries in the bones that we saw, I could not 100 per cent say they occurred in life; theoretically, they could have occurred after death. So we have to bear that in mind. Secondly, we had to accept that in this situation with lots of bodies put into a grave one on top of the other, often hundreds of bodies piled on top of each other and perhaps moved around afterwards and lorries going over the graves afterwards, that it was likely that some injuries would be caused after death; broken ribs, fractures of the face, perhaps of the pelvis. And we had to accept that and in a lot of the bodies we noted these; and where we did see these injuries, we accepted these as post-mortem injuries. So, anyway, what I'm trying to say, there is a difficulty in establishing from a skeleton injuries caused in life as opposed to injuries caused after death. One of the other difficulties was just because you have damage to bone doesn't necessarily mean that that's what killed this person. People don't -- you don't die from an injury to a bone; you die from the injuries to the tissues around about that, to the heart or to the brain or whatever. So we had to imply from particular damage to a bone that that would also cause internal damage, which I think in some situations is not unreasonable. Given that we were all pathologists used to practicing on fresh bodies, if you like, day to day, we know what surrounds these injuries, we know what effect they're going to have. So I think that was a reasonable assumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Just in relation to the fact that you were dealing with bones a lot of the time, in that regard did the role of the anthropologist become perhaps more significant than it otherwise would be in your -- in your usual, everyday work?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, very much so. In our normal jurisdictions, we -- it's uncommon to have an anthropologist working with us. The anthropologists were very useful. They provided two roles; first of all, to assist in trying to age the person from the skeleton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, secondly, in helping us interpret damage to bones saying sort of agreement that yes, we think that is a genuine bullet injury or that occurred after death or whatever. So it was a sort of consensual opinion, and there was seldom much different.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You have just answered my next question, which was that in circumstances where there may be some conflict between the two of you as to what was the appropriate cause of death, would it be the pathologist's opinion that would be superior, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would be. But I really cannot recall a situation in which that -- that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That there was that conflict?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there wasn't a conflict. If there was a conflict, we would all get together, all the anthropologists and pathologists together, and discuss it as you would do at any routine case. So there was certainly no conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Can I ask you this, Doctor, the fact that you were often dealing with skeletal remains, did that make it impossible to glean or to have some indication as to how long the remains had been buried for?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean what we all learned from the exercise, we learned that bodies decompose at different rates and in different conditions. Sometimes we had, dealing with bodies which at had allegedly been in the ground for five or six years and with a lot of tissue on them conversely, some bodies perhaps only six months almost reduced to skeleton, so there is a considerable variability. So it was difficult to give a precise estimate.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, I'm not -- I'm not criticising you at all. From reviewing each of your reports, there is no specific -- well, I'll rephrase that. You don't address that particular question in any of your reports. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And can I ask, is that because prior to your involvement in these autopsies, you had already received the information that these bodies, as you just said, had allegedly been in the ground for five or six years; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is fair, entirely fair, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Again, I'm not -- really you had an assumption --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- in your mind, prior to performing the autopsies that these were remains that had been buried for five or six years?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So there was no independent assessment to undermine that assumption, if you like?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No, okay. Did you -- in the same vein, did you receive, I suppose, some briefing from an investigator involved with the ICTY, Mr. Ruez, perhaps before you were involved in the autopsies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not usually specific though. I mean it was remarkably little information fed to us, which is, in -- you could say is quite a good thing. Apart --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps we would say, the Defence probably would say that is a good thing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, pathologists would say as well. There is argument whether we should be -- do a case sort of blind or with some information. I think there is a happy medium. I think we probably reached this here, and certainly we had little detailed information about the cases. Other than to the extent that we were generally informed whether this was a primary grave or whether this was a grave which had been disturbed, and that explained why so many of the bodies were disrupted. Things like that. But in terms of what weapons had been used, whether grenades had been used or whatever, we were the main instigators of that information from our findings.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that you were informed in a general sense as to the perceived circumstances under which these victims had met their deaths?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That's fair, okay. So it wasn't a case where you would come to it with equally as open that these were potentially victims in a combat situation, as equally as victims in alleged executions; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That it was more, in your mind, the balance weighed in favour of the fact that these were people who had been the victims of an alleged execution?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the more we went on into the particular grave sites, then the more we were emphasized in that notion.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That it was confirmed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by find ligatures and blindfolds an et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, we received your working notes, Doctor, and I just want -- I have a quick question in relation to them. They are, as you just indicated to the Prosecutor, they are summaries of all the individual autopsy reports from each of the sites that you were involved with, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I was in charge of, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. And you, obviously, read all of the autopsy reports themselves?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Just -- are they autopsy reports that you at some stage have provided to the Prosecution, or you can't answer that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These were all the reports that each pathologist compiled with the original notes. There are rough notes, as well. They were given to the Tribunal. I had copies made of everything at the time, in the mortuary, because I knew I was going to have to refer to them, and so I have everything that they have.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. So copies of the actual autopsy reports themselves have been given to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the originals. The signed originals, they have.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, just also in relation to the term that's used in your reports, the minimum number of persons, which is, as I understand it, that's more in the anthropologist's realm, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I've used that term very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps, I've misrepresented the situation there; perhaps you haven't used it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't my role to establish that. I could foresee so many difficulties. My role was to interpret the injuries and causes of death. And by worrying about minimum number of individuals, that was going to cause problems, so I specifically confined my observations to just what we could define as solid bodies or full bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the numbers I have produced in anything, they are -- actually the anthropologists should be able to give slightly higher numbers when taking into account body parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it's a difficult area and I felt the easiest thing was just to ignore these additional cases and for the purposes of interpreting injuries, to restrict myself to bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Can I ask you which anthropologists, if any, did you deal with in relation to the calculation of numbers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The senior anthropologist when I was there in the first year was Jose-Pablo Baraybar, who I believe is giving evidence; then we had an American, Shella Morton [phoen] and Cheryl Kismartsik [phoen]; and finally, the final year was Erin Kimmerle. So they were the sort of chief anthropologists, if you like, and they were responsible for establishing minimum numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: If you feel you can, are you able to make any comment at all about the reliability of the process of establishing minimum number of persons from body parts or is that your realm?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- nothing constructive to add to that. That's not really my role.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Maybe I'll leave it there then. Can I take you then to your first report, Doctor, that's the -- that's P575, Your Honour. You have a copy of that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But perhaps if it could be shown on e-court, Your Honour, that would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, you have that there, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 1999, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Now, just say from the outset, I don't propose to ask you about any graves where blindfolds and ligatures were found. So you can focus your mind on those ones where they weren't located. What I would like to ask you about in respect of the 1999 report, okay. If we go to page --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: 13, yes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Nova Kasaba. So just to make sure that it's unambiguous, that this is a grave where there were -- now, what you've said at page 13 is that clothing was present, none had blindfolds; and apart from one possible, none had ligatures binding their wrists. Now, is that your interpretation, that there was possibly one ligature, or is that information you've received from somebody else?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our interpretation. I can't remember the details, but I imagine it was probably a bit of cloth lying loosely with the body, which we possibly interpreted that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Then under injuries, you've got observations about the bodies at NK04, and what I'm interested in particular is your observation that the majority of the bodies in NK04, or perhaps -- no, I'm misreading it. What you say is the majority of those that did not have gunshot injuries were from NK04, which may or may not be of significance. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm -- I remember writing that, but I'm not sure if I can find it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. It's still on page 13 under the heading "injuries."

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, I've got your -- and perhaps if you go to your working notes from NK04, I don't know how easy it will be for you to locate them.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very easy.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. You've got them? Is that got on the right-hand side, NK04 B and BP?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. So if we go through your working notes for NK04, there are a number, I count 16, unascertained causes of death out of 38 bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. And that's where that observation comes from, that there was a majority that didn't have gunshot injuries. Now --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be strictly fair, that's the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slightly different is the number with gunshot injuries --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because you can have a gunshot injury --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That's not fatal.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that actually would be non-fatal. They are much the same, but just for record that's what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Is it the case that when you -- you had that observation, that it may or may not be of significance, is that a matter that it's open, what you are asked by the Prosecutor, it's open to interpret those injuries as having been sustained in the course of combat or conflict?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I follow that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, when you have the cause of death as unascertained?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Then it's open -- it may be a non-fatal. Is that your word?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be non-fatal.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Could be non-fatal?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And, again, that is something that may well be consistent with it having been inflicted in combat?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You see what I mean?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it may be non-fatal. It would have to be -- I mean there weren't many, if at all, who did have gunshot injuries in which I still gave the cause of death as unascertained. I would have to go through them but certainly not very many. In that case, we would have to be speaking of gunshot injuries perhaps to soft tissues only. So yes, it is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Ms. Condon, if you could tell me how I can locate NK04 details.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are working notes that have been supplied to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which we don't have.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Which the Court doesn't have. Perhaps the Prosecution may well have copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Or the alternative is we could have a copy placed on the ELMO, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's okay. Next time if it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, there is also just in relation to -- before we leave your working notes for NK04, there is observations in the far right column where -- do you see where you've written"shotgun pellets embedded in skull?"

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And then underneath that "possible blunt force trauma" for the next case?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the next case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, I will return to the shotgun pellets in the skull, that's something I want to ask you about a little bit later. Now, in relation to NK04, which is another grave, you also make the observation that "the average number of bullet injuries there was 3.2." That's at the bottom of page 13. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, again, as I understand the general consensus, the -- in conflict or in combat, it's usually a higher number of shots per individual. Is that correct? That's what you expect to find?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I know the exact basis of that. You could argue that yes, there would be larger numbers of shots, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Right, okay. Well, I think in the Krstic trial you were asked similar questions by the Prosecutor, and you -- you indicated that the research does indicate that you -- you would usually find a larger number of shots per person in battle, whether non-fatal or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So, in NK08, not NK04, you made the observation that there is an average of 3.2.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Is that again something that you would put into the assessment of whether or not you would exclude the victims in that grave as having been as a result of conflict?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might be. On the other hand, the difference between the two is actually quite small, and the number of cases we're dealing with is pretty small as well, so I'm not sure how statistically significant all that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. If I can take you now to page 14, so if you go over the page, and under the heading "weapons used." Now, if I can just make this general observation about all three of your reports, Doctor: It's correct to say, isn't it, that your assessment is that the majority of the gunshot injuries are as the result of high velocity weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: However, under the heading "weapons used," here in the second paragraph, you do make the observation that a handgun may have been used in one case because of the limited degree of damage to the bones?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And then you say "either that or the bullet had passed through something else beforehand such that it's lost its energy?"

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Does that indicate to you or is it open to interpret that as a result of there being a considerable distance between the shooter and the target?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be not -- a third possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You accept that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have to be quite a long distance, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But that's again when we transpose that into a warfare, conflict, combat situation, that of itself would not be extraordinary?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Ms. Condon, please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can the microphone be raised?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a short one. I think Mr. Meek and I have the same problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to jump around a little bit, Doctor, and I now want to take you to an observation you made in your third report, which is page 2446, so this is the 2001 season. Do you have it, page 2446? And at page 4, paragraph 2, this is an observation you have made in all of your reports, but it relates to the difficulty in distinguishing between a gunshot wound or a shrapnel wound. You see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Can you -- well, perhaps can you assist the Trial Chamber, what is that difficulty and how did it apply here?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The high velocity bullet hitting a bone will cause a lot of fragmentation of bone, so will a bit of shrapnel. In the ideal situation, we can tell the difference because we see a nice round hole from a bullet, and the fractures radiating from it. Similarly, in the shrapnel injury, you find much more rugged edges to the defect without a nice central hole, and, hopefully, there will be bits of shrapnel around the region. So if we saw that, we were fairly confident in saying that one of the other. There is a sort of grey area in between, however, in which bullets don't cause classic damage to bones; and shrapnel injuries, perhaps it's only one small bit which may begin to act like a bullet. So there was a sort of -- sometimes -- we may well have gotten some of them wrong. I admit that, but I don't think it's a huge number.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there was other -- sufficient other evidence in these bodies, particularly with finding pieces of shrapnel, finding damage to adjacent tissues. So you get a sort of regional, regional damage rather than say specifically just a bullet going through the arm; and some evidence, some evidence on the clothing, perhaps burning on the clothing. So putting all these together, I think we got probably the majority of the interpretation correct in shrapnel versus gun shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Dr. Clark, could you possibly be more specific here when you say the majority or I don't think it's a huge number. Is it -- is it possible to give us a more accurate picture by -- by percentages, by indicating percentages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because the majority, if it's 51 as against 49, it's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I accept that. I would think it's in the 70 or 80s, 80 per cent, that sort of region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps, we haven't really established this: In the context of conflict or combat, are you able to say what is more common in terms of injury? Is it shrapnel injury sustained as a result of shrapnel or is it injuries sustained as a result of gunshot?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In typical war situations, major conflicts, it has been shown that the greatest number of injuries are caused by explosions, so that would -- that would include shrapnel, yes, as opposed to gunshot injuries. That has been shown in really every modern conflict and is a well-established principle.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As is the fact that you always get more, far more wounded people than killed people. So these are two sort of basic principles which have been established in major conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. Can I ask you this: If -- in a scenario which I suspect you had regularly where there was no soft tissue to give --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- obviously a more reliable indication, and all you had was the bone itself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And it was ambiguous, as I'm sure it often is in your --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- profession as to which of the two it was --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- gunshot, shrapnel, would you tend to adopt the conclusion it was gunshot? Would you favour that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we would. I think we did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. And is that because of what I asked you right at the beginning, just simply because in your mind that would be consistent with what you were told about the execution scenario?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean on some bodies we had definite gunshot injuries and definite shrapnel on the same body. I suppose we were working on the principle that the largest number of injuries on these bodies were gunshot injuries. So we tended to favour --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That general --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- what was the commonest as opposed to what was least common.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. Can I ask you about just generally trauma to the bone? Is it -- is it fair to say there's -- there's -- relevant here, there's three types of trauma that we could talk about. There's blunt trauma?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: There's sharp trauma?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And there's projectile -- trauma sustained as a result of a projectile?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Obviously, in that term projectile, we're including bullets and shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Of course. Now, I want to ask you about the difficulties that you have observed in distinguishing whether or not bone trauma is a result of blunt trauma or projectile trauma. That's -- that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And, again, can you assist the Trial Chamber, where is the difficulty in that distinction and how did it apply here?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, we will have an ideal situation in which a gunshot injury will produce a hole, a defect.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I am listening, I'm sorry. I was just saying something to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ideal situation, again, pretty easy; the gunshot injury will cause a hole in the bone with fractures around about. A blunt force trauma will tend to produce just a line, a fracture, not on the surface, but just a line without actually producing an internal defect. The difficulty did come, for instance, on fractures of the skull, which they were of a shape and situation which we often see in our normal practice as caused by blunt force, somebody being struck on the head or falling. They occur on typical sites and that's what we're used to seeing, and I would interpret that as blunt force trauma. You could argue that this could be caused by perhaps a bullet striking lesser energy at an odd angle and could conceivably produce a fracture like that. So that is a possibility. But just from my general pathology experience, because we see far more blunt trauma than gunshot injury in normal practice, I interpreted them as blunt force trauma.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. But here you had the double -- the added obstacle, I should say, of assessing whether or not it's --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Post-mortem, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And let me ask you this: Is it possible for a bone to fracture without actually being touched by the projectile? Can that happen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't think it does. I think it's extremely rare.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Right, okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But it technically can happen; it can go through the soft tissue?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can go through soft tissues, but my understanding, and I read about this recently, it's very unusual for a bone to fracture from a bullet going through soft tissue.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Without the bullet actually touching the bone?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: If that's an extremely rare scenario, I wouldn't ask you about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. I will show you some photos then, and we will just -- perhaps I'll ask for your interpretation as to these.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could have a look at P -- no, actually. P0214, if we could have that up. Nothing? I have the 65 ter number as P597. The P number on the exhibit list I have is P0214. That's not it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I see it's P02149 on the list I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Sorry. There is a 9, sorry. My mistake. Thank you. My mistake. Thank you, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You have that in front of you. Now, this is a injury that you described as damage to the bone caused by a blunt instrument. Sorry, well that's the description I have of it on the exhibit list. You accept that as a description you are responsible for, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. Can I ask you this: Is it also open to interpret that injury to the bone as the sort of injury you would see sustained by a shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be. I mean I do remember -- because these cases were quite unusual.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And when we did see something like this --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Not to interrupt you, but we should establish this is from Glogova?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Glogova, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Glogova number 5. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we usually got together, the anthropologists, plural, and the pathologists and would discuss this in some detail. Now, I agree this could be a shrapnel injury, but we must have taken the view that this was most likely blunt force trauma, I think possibly on the basis we presumably found no shrapnel at all on the body. And we felt this fitted the best interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. But you would accept, would you not, that --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't exclude that being --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No. Because in the same way that even if you don't find the bullet in the body or the shrapnel in the body, that of course is not conclusive as to whether or not that --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- that has been in fact the cause of the injury.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think because we were seeing such large numbers of cases that after a while you got a feeling that this is slightly different, and that's why we probably interpreted that as that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Can I show you P02134. Perhaps we should, for the record, this is from Kozluk grave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, again, perhaps if you can just indicate to the Trial Chamber, that rather neat, round hole on the right, that's obviously what is interpreted as the bullet hole. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, if I could just -- then there is the fracturing that occurs from --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, the bullet hole is at number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just below the letter 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the fracture lines are going forward and also downwards where the white material is just below.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Perhaps just to the left there is an irregular -- do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, again, given that it's an irregular fracture, it's an irregular hole, in fact, is that the sort of injury that you can exclude as having been sustained as a result of a shrapnel injury?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's -- it would be very unlikely if it was shrapnel injury, it would be assuming that two projectiles hit the skull exactly at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because when one hits it, the rest -- all the bones around about are going to be shattered. I think what we've got here, that this is just a small portion of the fracture, which we have not been able to recover. I think you've got to bear in mind that this skull originally was in fragments. This has been stuck together by glue, so this is the end result reconstructed. And we will -- small bits of bone will fall out. So don't believe for a moment that that skull has stayed completely intact. It has been in multiple bits. The anthropologists have glued it together and have identified this nice, round hole, and with fracture lines running from it. I don't think that is a shrapnel injury.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Just in relation to what I asked you before about the assessment as -- of the majority of the injuries having been sustained as of high-velocity rifles, now, is that information that you were given by -- as a result of a ballistics experts or is that something that you assessed yourselves?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We assessed ourselves on the bases of the nature of the fracturing, the extreme amount of damage with the central hole and radiating fractures and a huge exit and, secondly, on the finding of typical high velocity bullets in the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But again, another quite -- or no, I will withdraw that. Another limitation that you faced yourself in the interpretation of those injuries was that you were simply not in a position, were you, to assess the distance at which the target had been from the shooter. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, we couldn't assess that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Whether short range, long-range, simply impossible?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, I -- I now want to take you back to your 1999 report, and ask you about Konjevic Polje. That's at page 17, please. Do you have that in front of you, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And I'll just go through, summarise the findings in relation to this grave. No blindfolds or ligatures, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Clothing present on everyone, and as you indicated at the outset, no traditional military clothing as you could ascertain?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah. There was one female victim, which is obviously unusual?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: There was a makeshift stretcher in the grave. There was no -- the -- sorry. The average number of shots were three per person?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And there were some non-gunshot injuries which included a fractured skull and fractures of some arm bones and ribs. Now, in relation to all of those factors, are you in a position to exclude the possibility that the victims in that grave died in combat?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. And I just want to ask you very quickly about -- I said from the outset I wouldn't ask you about anything where blindfolds and ligatures had been found, but I'm going to go back on that. Just quickly at page 21 of your 1999 report where you make some observations about Glogova, and you make the observation that there had been -- you say that the paragraph beginning, "Injuries to the trunk."

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And then you go on to say that there had been shots to the head, to the back of the head, and fired from behind perhaps with the victim standing upright or kneeling down. Now, it's fair to say, isn't it, that you are speculating there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it was a common -- a common feature amongst these -- these cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Where you found what could be described as a random pattern of firing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Which I think is in fact words you used in your report, again, would a random pattern of firing be more consistent with conflict or combat?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be one conclusion. There could be other conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's open.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, just finally, I want to take you back to your 2001 report. Okay. So this is -- okay. Now, again, if we focus on the findings in relation to Ravnice, Ravnice was not a grave as such, was it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was bodies found on an embankment, a steep slope.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And not buried?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not buried.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And just your findings there. You indicated that again clothing was still present; again, you make the observation none of it military in the traditional sense of the term, you mean that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: A uniform?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. That's page 6. That's the second-last paragraph on page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you indicated that none of the clothing showed any signs of burning. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, with shrapnel or grenade injuries, is it often a secondary consequence of that that you do have burning?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. But again the absence of that is not conclusive of the fact that they are not injuries sustained as a result of shrapnel; is it, it may or may not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- yes. Yes, it doesn't completely exclude it. You could get a shrapnel injury to the head and there is no clothing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you did find a person who had some pistol bullets in his jacket pocket?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And the state of the decomposition of the bodies, now were you able to determine how long these bodies had been exposed to the elements for?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in any detail, but normal practice would say at least -- at least probably a year or two years.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Though fully skeletonised?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fully skeletonised, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And in terms of -- I appreciate the difficulty with making the commitment to whether or not something is pre- or post-mortem damage, given the state?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But there would have been, no doubt, exposure to animals in that period?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There could have been. There wasn't a great deal -- I mean animals normally cause specific types of damage to bones. You can see nibbling marks. I think we saw that a few times but certainly not a major -- a very frequent basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this was -- this was an area as well that you did make the observation that the direction of shooting was suggestive of a random pattern of firing, and that's an observation you make at page 7?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And in fact you said only ten of the 176 men died of a single shot to the head?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. So, again, bearing in mind the factors that we've gone through in relation to the findings at Ravnice, you cannot exclude the victims there having been injured or died as a result of combat, can you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure there are other interpretation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. And, finally, we go to Zeleni Jadar. It begins at page 23 of your report, and you make the observation under clothing that in several cases there was evidence of burning.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, in the reverse, that's something that you would -- you may well expect to see as a result of shrapnel --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- damage?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some of these bodies we did find what we interpreted as shrapnel injuries, plus shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Itself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Were you able -- I'll take you to that specific finding. That's at page 25, and you said the bulk of injuries were bullet injuries. There were clear blast injuries in seven men?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah. Again -- well, and can I ask you just in relation to those two factors alone, that we've just observed, the blast injuries and the clothing having been burnt, again, that would be -- those would be factors that would weigh in favour of the possibility that these are victims that have died in the course of conflict. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, that's one possibility, yes, but there are others as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. But it's open?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's open.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Open on the findings?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Just pardon me a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Condon, and I thank you, Dr. Clark. According to the information that we have, the Borovcanin Defence team would like to cross-examine this witness. Is that correct, Mr. Lazarevic or Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as all the teams of the Defence agreed, we are not going to question this witness. We will be questioning the next witness. So I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that we do not have questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I also wish to confirm this with you, Madam Fauveau, because you had indicated you required ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Yes, I stick to my ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So go ahead. We will have a break at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, yesterday, in page 86 of the transcript, you stated that the purpose of your work was to identify wounds and to establish causes of death. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the prime function.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you added that you were trying to recuperate, to retrieve all other evidence that could be found on the bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that the analysis of residual earth that could have been found in the bodies and their clothing could have shown where the people were killed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- that's a possibility. I -- I understood, however, that any soil analysis of these cases was done at the grave site. There was a soil analyst involved, and he was doing this at the grave site rather than at the mortuary.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you know whether, with regard to the bodies you examined, whether such analysis was performed and whether there was a comparison of the soil found in Potocari? Do you know whether this was done or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the details. I do know, and I met the soil analyst, that he was able to link certain bodies with certain sites. I don't know about Potocari specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you do not know either anything about Bratunac? You never heard that there was a soil analysis made in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In your report on season 2000, page 24 - this is Exhibit P598, page 24 - you mentioned the grave in Glogova, and you said that most bodies found in that grave would have been killed in the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say they were killed; I say they are alleged to have been killed there. There is a difference there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That's right. I may not have been very accurate in my question. Indeed, there was -- there were some analysis carried out in the Kravica warehouse, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of -- I'm sorry, of -- analysis of?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let me reformulate my question. Is it fair to say that in the Kravica warehouse some human residue, some human rests were found?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. We -- two small pieces of bone were recovered and pieces of tooth, and I examined these and established what they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'm interested in knowing whether similar analysis of human remains were performed somewhere else in Kravica in the market, in the supermarket in Kravica, or in any other place in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware -- certainly, I was never asked to examine any tissue in the whole three years that I was there. I'm not aware that other material was -- was discovered.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to confirm with the other Defence teams that none of you would like to cross-examine this witness any further. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, good morning. I would like to ask some questions on a limited basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can start now and within six minutes we will have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions. I reviewed your reports, and I wondered if you could help me clarify some issues. You stated in your 1999 report that there was a "varying criteria." Can you tell me sir what you mean by that varying criteria?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in reference to...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Proof of gunshot injury.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes, as I have explained earlier, this was very easy. There is a classic hole; there was a bullet with the wound. That was easy. Other times there was perhaps not a classic hole, but some bullet residue, and we still established that as gunshot injury. On other occasions the evidence was less convincing, but we took the view that this most likely was a gunshot injury. Anything below that we excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you reduced that to an opinion of being unascertained, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, what is the varying levels of certainty that you applied in, again, these proof of gunshot injuries analyses that you performed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, really as I have said, I mean if it was a classic hole, central hole with are radiating fractures, that was absolutely had to be a gunshot injury. So we were very certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, what I'm asking, to understand your report better, and if you look at page 4, paragraph 3, you talk about the diagnosis of gunshot damage was based on varying criteria on varying levels of certainty. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just highlight for me what those levels of certainty are, in your analysis as a pathologist?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first one was, as I said, when there was a classic hole and there was a bullet there; there was absolutely no problem with it, a bullet fragments.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What would we call that? A no problem level of certainty?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Next one?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next one would be there was no bullet fragment as all, but there was a very typical bullet fragment defect in the bone, and that would be pretty certain as well. The third one was when we had fracturing, not necessarily a classic bullet injury but with bullet fragments around about, and we interpreted that as a bullet injury. Less than that, if was an untypical form of fracture, and there was no bullet fragments, then we said that that was not -- well, we didn't state that that was a bullet injury. Some of them may well have been, but we did not state that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you, in your report, base your opinion on a reasonable degree of pathological certainty and medical certainty?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think you can see that we have erred a lot on the side of doubt and caution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so I can understand the whole exhumation process and the autopsies performed, how many -- I know you made a distinction between bodies and I think today you even used the word solid or complete bodies. But in your report, you refer to a distinction between bodies and parts of bodies, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just describe that for me, again, so I appreciate it a little better?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We took as a body any remains which were what you would call a person, that was -- in other words, the whole of the trunk, and the head, but perhaps the legs were missing. But we took that as a -- as a person. If it was a whole body with the trunk and the legs, but the head was missing, we would still call that a body. If it was just a limb, a leg, or just a chest, part of the chest, we would call that a body part.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Out of those autopsies, how many autopsies did you and your team perform in connection with all the bodies that were exhumed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's over 3.000, that's including the body parts. We -- the figure for bodies for the Srebrenica cases was about 1100.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So at any point were there 7.000 or so exhumed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At any point, sir, were there any -- from either the exhumations conducted by the ICTY or the local Bosnian Commission for Tracing Missing Persons, have they ever uncovered more than 7.000 bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what has happened since 2001. Certainly, in the time I was there, I think the total body figure, according to my reports, for the Srebrenica sites was about 1100.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just in the minute or two, so I can understand, because we heard some testimony from someone I think who was involved in your team, Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez, it is my recollection - and I can cite the report for counsel - that he says that 96 per cent of all the graves have been exhumed. Would you agree or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I kind of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. This is a misstatement of any evidence this Court has heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will cite the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And cite it within a time frame, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will. The testimony is on September 15, 2006 on page 1731, and I will just give a little preliminary before you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I was asked in 2003, line 3, and on. "In 2003, isn't it correct that was your opinion with respect to exhumations you said, 'We are now in 2003. Eight years after the events. We have located probably 90 per cent of all of these graves.'" "Q. Do you remember giving that statement in the Blagojevic case, page 729, lines 9 through 12? "A. Yes, correct? "Q. Now, we are even more removed, three years or more; correct? "A. Yes. "Q. What per cent does it increase or decrease that I can use? "A. Only one site has been found since 1993. It is a site located in Potocari that was discovered by the team of Mr. Masovic. This is so maybe we are now at 96 per cent." Line 14 he ends with that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait one moment, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The objection stands. He is clearly talking number about the number of graves found at that time of that testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness has told you he can only confirm as regards 2001, not beyond that. So there is no point in indicating to him what other witnesses may -- may think or may believe amounts to -- is further excavations or burial sites found after that. So please let's move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with the demographer that's working with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The, sorry, demographer?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Heleg Brunborg. If Heleg Brunbor, in his report, would state to this Court that - and that is on page 3 of his report - "the total number of victims not known. Exhumations conducted by the ICTY and the local Bosnian Commission for Tracing Missing Persons have uncovered more than 7.000 bodies out of the (broadly defined) Srebrenica territory." Is that perhaps, sir, with all due respect to Mr. Brunborg, an exaggeration?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. All I can say the bodies I was involved with have, as I've totaled them up, are 1100 bodies; including body parts, perhaps up to 1500. I don't know. But what happened after that, I have no idea at all. I have nothing do with the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons. I had nothing to do with locating or establishing grave sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this before we take this next break. Did you, sir, at any time state that there were 4.000 bodies that were exhumed and autopsies conducted on them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know where that information would have come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we take the break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, do you have further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought so. So we will have a 25-minute break. And then we'll finish with this witness. The next witness is a protected one, so we will need time for making the necessary preparations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, just to follow up on a couple of points, and I recognise that your reports were done in 1999, 2000, and 2001.
