Did you obtain any information since leaving the ICTY, the Office of the Prosecution, with respect to the number of exhumation that is were done or any further autopsy that is were performed after you left?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that ICTY, the Tribunal had not conducted any further investigations. But I am generally aware, being in contact with [unknown name], that the Bosnian commission were reviewing sites, but I know nothing of the details or numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, on page 44, right before the break, I asked you the question if at any time you stated that there were 4.000 bodies that were exhumed and autopsies conducted on them. And your answer on line 18 says, "No, I don't know where that information would have come from." And let me ask you this: You never would have said that, why?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- because I physically haven't done 4.000 autopsies on the Srebrenica cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And because it's not true, correct? If you could have written that, it would have been something you wouldn't do, and the reason you wouldn't write 4.000 is simply because it's not true, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that other people have done autopsies on other cases, so the numbers -- it's not just my evidence; it's other people as well, but I would be surprised if the number was 4.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So was I. Do you write -- in your position as a pathologist and a doctor, do you write in the medical literature at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And did you ever write an article entitled, "Pathological Investigation" in the War Crimes Pathological Investigation Review, I guess or journal?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I know what you are speaking about. It is an international text-book and that was two articles I was invited to contribute to. So I suspect that you are going to tell me that I put the 4.000 figure there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you did?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but all I would say to that is that I was involved not just in the Srebrenica sites, of course, there were other graves in Bosnia as well. And that may have been -- I think I may have obtained some information from other sources and that was perhaps a round figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When I write I usually footnote if I obtain information from other sources. Did you footnote that, that it this wasn't you yourself conducted or did you cite that this was from other sources?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't -- no, I didn't cite that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me quote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Is it possible to have the witness read what is claimed that he said, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Mr. Ostojic, can you be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will try, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On page 365 of that article, which I see you have with you, on the right-hand column, first full paragraph, because the paragraph carries over from the left-hand column, it starts -- first let me establish that's your article, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And this was written in 2005, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. It says, "From the first sites explored in 1996 until the end of 2001, some 4.000 to 5.000 bodies were exhumed, but there are many graves still to be exhumed and probably still -- and probably many still to be discovered." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't actually found that page yet, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's page 365. I don't think you --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Left-hand column -- I mean right-hand column, first full paragraph, because it carries over.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It starts with the words, "From the first sites explored in 1996 until the end of 2001, some 4.000 to 5.000 bodies were examined." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Examined or exhumed? Because before in the transcript at line 12, you are reported as saying exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I may have misspoke, Your Honour. It is clearly examined, but I think the doctor can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is "examined." I must have gained that information from -- from somewhere. I suspect I may have contacted the Bosnian commission at some stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, in your notes or your file or even your memory, do you recall that at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it, but I mean it says -- it says -- it's a reasonably specific figure and I wouldn't have put a specific figure, had I not had some bases for it. Bear in mind it's not just Srebrenica cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just pardon me a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I am being asked the following. I appreciate the Court's indulgence and my learned colleagues. Just when we came back from the break you said you don't have any of that information on page 45 the Bosnian authorities. So I want you to reconcile it for me. Do you have the information, don't you have the information, is this an exaggeration, did you write it, didn't you write it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I have written this, I will accept that. These figures must have come from some --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I hate to interrupt. Don't speculate. If you know tell us; if you don't, tell us you don't?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got the figure down there, although I cannot remember the specific source for that. It may have been a website, but I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's talk about your objectivity for a moment. Sir, we have talked with my learned friend for the Defence of Mr. Popovic about the limitations on the pathological evidence and you shared that; it's in your report. Now, the contributions that pathological evidence are what? What's your goal when you go in there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is to -- with a body, my goal is to establish that this is a human body, it's to establish how much of the body is there, to identify injuries and any illness on the body, to retrieve any evidence from the body, which may be of further use.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Is your goal ever to obtain evidence for a criminal conviction?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I am -- it's my job as a forensic pathologist to obtain evidence for a criminal conviction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Isn't -- thank you. Is it your job also as a forensic pathologist to refute any evidence in order to obtain an acquittal or is it strictly looking at it to obtain criminal convictions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I obtain the evidence, and it's up to others to interpret from that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's look at page 367 of your article; same article, left-hand column. You specifically state what the autopsy is being carried out for. You see it, the lower portion, last paragraph on the left-hand column?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It says, "As indicated at the start of this section, the autopsy is being carried both to obtain evidence for a criminal conviction and to try to establish the identity of the body." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In fact, isn't it true, that in your job with the ICTY Office of the Prosecution, your main focus was -- or the primary focus was the former, to obtain criminal convictions, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us, if you examined any evidence to refute any of the theories that were shared to you by the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't actually put to me any particular theories.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any information or knowledge that you, sir, would conclude that there were allegedly 7.000 massacred in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is just -- that is general knowledge that I have. I haven't refuted that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, what efforts have you made, sir, to establish that the victims in Srebrenica, in July, may have been -- may have died as a result of combat casualty?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have tried to establish the information from the bodies as openly and independently as possible, and it's for others to interpret that. We've gone through that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 364 of your article, right-hand column. You see where it starts with, "Former Yugoslavia"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you state there without any footnotes again in the medical literature publication, "7.000 men were massacred at Srebrenica in 1995." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What's the bases of your opinion, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is information which is -- has been generally presented. It's in -- it's information that the Tribunal has given to me at various stages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who at the Tribunal gave you that? I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having been around working in this area for three years here, it's information which one just gathers from various people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. So it's speculation, would that be fair to characterise it as that? You have no proof of it, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not individually, I'm repeating what has been established elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm just talking to you about you individually, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no -- I have no idea how many -- how many bodies there are, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this, if we can talk a little bit about -- we talked about body and body parts, and thank you for that. So I can understand the difference between a decomposed body and a skeletonised body, can you tell us the difference between the two?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A decomposed body is a body one which is not fresh and is starting to disintegrate, and the end result of that is a skeleton.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it fair that doing an autopsy as a pathologist, it's very difficult, nearly impossible, to assess the cause of death on a decomposed body?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And is it also true that with a skeletonised body, it is virtually impossible to determine the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fair, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What's fair, it's in your report, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm just regurgitating to you what's in your report. My question to you, sir, on the analysis you have done is can you tell me from the 1100 or 1500 autopsies you have conducted or your team, how many were decomposed and how many were skeletonised?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All were decomposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Because skeletonised includes the decomposed as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's a subgroup of that, right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly, it's the end result of it. The actual number of skeletonised, I can't give you the exact figure. It must have been approaching 40 to 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Is it true that the decomposed remains, it's virtually impossible to be certain that any of the injuries found have necessarily occurred in life or antemortem, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, when we talked about briefly this morning about shrapnel injuries, you use it I think in your report as a synonym with fragmentation, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever do a percentage to determine how many of the bodies you examined, sir, or body parts resulted from fragmentation or shrapnel injuries?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the figure at hand, but I could work it out. Out of the whole 1100 case, it could be probably no more than 5 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But Do you agree with me, sir, as a pathologist, that fragmentation or shrapnel injuries can sometimes closely resemble those caused by bullets?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's answered that already. He had several questions put to him on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think it was more specific, but I will move on, Your Honour. I just had one other question on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Condon's cross-examination dealt with that extensively.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know that, Your Honour. I just -- they were noting that I should slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not only that it closely resembles shrapnel and fragmentation closely resemble injuries caused by bullets; but given that they were decomposed bodies and skeletonised bodies, it makes it even more difficult to make that assessment, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I want to talk a little bit about blast injuries. Can you tell me what that is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are injuries that are -- it's a term used to describe injuries caused by an exploding device.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In the end result, I think we know, although with all due respect to your medical background, a blast injury can result in loss of a limb, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Or loss of a body part, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, at any time evaluate why some of the corpses, if I could call them that, with all due respect, and some of the evidence that you reviewed, that those missing body parts were a result of blast injuries?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them may well have been, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you give me the percentage of how many?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic, and Dr. Clark, you are moving too fast. Please allow -- you both speak the same language, or almost. So I suggest you allow a pause, a short pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The figures are in my sheets, my working sheets. I could work them out if required. But certainly some of the body parts did have shrapnel damage on them, a small proportion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the specific shrapnel damage on small proportions. I'm talking about the autopsies you conducted on the actual corpses, as you call the solid or full body corpses. I think you just call it body, as opposed to body parts, just so we're on the same page. Of those, how many were full corpses or full bodies and those that you have examined or your team?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We examined approximately 1100 full bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. But I thought that the you said that out of those 1100 full bodies, there were some body parts missing, perhaps a limb or an arm or a leg?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've already explained. I think -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to go through this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand, but--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has explained that [indiscernible] or a body without a head. He's gone through this already.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Am I correct, sir, that the contributions of pathological evidence is to confirm specific allegations but equally important to refute them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, you said on pages -- page 7, lines 5 through 7 today, during your direct, I believe, "A large number of men did not fall in this category of being combat men." "We had young men," you say, "particularly we had a lot of elderly people." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What is your criteria for elderly people who cannot fight?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would imagine the same as most people. I'm speaking that there were a substantial number of people, let's say over the age of 65. Now, that's not it say that somebody aged 65 cannot fire a gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I understand --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just want to know what your criteria is for making that statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say some of the people in their 70s, 80s, I would call elderly, not the normal fighting man.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Similarly, on page 7, lines 15 through 17, you stated that from what you reviewed that the majority of shots killing some of these men came from behind, which is perhaps not what you would expect in a face-to-face conflict situation. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you know or learn of any ambushes that were undertaken in July of 1995 between the adverse parties?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with how an ambush works?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did any investigator or military consultant with the Office of the Prosecutor advise you of what their estimate is of those killed during the ambush?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you think that might be significant in your analysis in obtaining an objective opinion as to what the cause of death may be?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be, if it's put to me. If these scenarios are put to me, it's my job to say, well, that is consistent or that's inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me put it to you. Let a say there was one ambush in 1995, okay? Although there were more, let's just take the one. There was an ambush of 100 people. Where would you expect the injuries to be sustained from the people who were being ambushed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What could you -- can I ask you what you mean by "an ambush."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, there are soldiers that may be sitting in a ravine waiting for a section or group of people to pass; and then to make a surprise attack on them, once they have passed the actual direct line where they're sitting or waiting for them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the implication would be that they are shot from behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's the way you assume, sir, then that's what you assume?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said these are soldiers passing through, and after they've passed through they have been ambushed. If that's the scenario, yes, you would expect the bulk of shots from behind or from the side.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what if there was an ambush where they jumped in front of this group of men - although you called them soldiers - this group of men, and they started running, where do you think the injuries would be sustained by these people who were running away from the soldiers who ambushed them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, you would expect them in -- shots to the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you think that would be significant in your analysis to determine whether or not these people, as you write in your article, were killed as a result of a massacre or a result of combat action?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've -- I've provided the information. You are now providing scenarios, and I am accepting your scenario. It's up to others to, if they want, produce other scenarios.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. On page 22, line -- so let me -- before I go to that next question. Is it fair to say if there were three ambushes, that would be information that would you like to know to make a fair and more accurate assessment of the material that you reviewed, analysed; would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be interesting. There is a limit to what I can comment on. There is enormous variety of scenarios and possibilities, and I cannot go through each one in turn. All I will do is provide the basic information and let others question me on it, as you are doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, on page 22 today, line 17, you talked about, "High velocity bullet" - line 17, if you are following - and that's an inappropriate use of the term, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a -- it's a term of common usage.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But you -- isn't it true that wound from assault rifles and the like are often referred to as high velocity injuries but such terminology is not entirely appropriate?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And where do you think I got that from?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can find that I wrote that article in 2005 and these reports were written before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the information since your 2001 report, have you...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Ostojic, please slow down. Because we've got your question missing, to which there is an answer, or a part of an answer. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I can repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think for the transcript we need to go through it again. It's too fast, going too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I think, Doctor, it's my fault. I apologise. I think I asked you, "And where do you think I got that information?" It's not entirely appropriate to use the term high velocity bullet.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You got it from my article, but I think you will find that the high velocity injuries is a term used by a large number of people. Just in the way shrapnel is to some extent an inappropriate term, but it's -- most people know what we mean by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with respect to the information that you have since your 2001 report, have you been given any other data or information from other pathologists or anthropologists in connection with the events in Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you spoke a little bit earlier today about the wounded, and I think that you said that the ratio or I think you mentioned that there were fewer wounded men than dead, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you would expect in a conflict or a war situation that there would be a ratio of 3:1 from wounded to dead, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily 3:1, but higher than 1:1.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you stated in your report, and I think in your testimony, that you didn't see it -- those wounded men in the hospitals in and around Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information that that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, did you, as a pathologist, ask the Office of the Prosecutor to try to obtain that information from the hospitals in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Not specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you know that a column was leaving Srebrenica and going towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know if any -- did they show you any video or anything of men arriving at what they called the safe zone or the free territory, showing that they were injured and they were carrying injured people?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you procure from the Bosnian authorities, sir, any medical documentation or information to confirm that there were fewer wounded than dead as a result of the Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Ostojic, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, obtain or seek, excuse me, did you seek from the Prosecutor at all to obtain such information from the Bosnian authorities?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, seek from the Prosecution or on your own information from the ABiH military authorities to determine how many wounded men there were as a result of this military column moving from Srebrenica to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecutors had my reports. They did not raise that issue at all either with me. The -- if they had that information, then it was up to them to raise that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But you never sought it out. Why didn't you seek it out, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not -- that wasn't actually -- I don't think it's actually recorded in my reports about these. It's recorded in the testimony. I was not asked to consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would it have any impact on your analysis in your report at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I was informed that there were thousands of injured parties, yes, I would -- it wouldn't necessarily affect my report, what it stated in the report. It might affect my questioning and answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think it would affect your report, with all due respect, and I'm suggesting to you it would have affected it in that you wouldn't have concluded, as you did in many of the cases that, they were from simple bullet injuries not related to combat. I think that might be significant, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect, my report is about bodies that I examined. It's not about the whole conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting the whole conflict, but of the bodies that you examined?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bodies I examined, we found a very small number with signs of previous -- previous wounds; in other words, bandages around the limbs. That was an extremely small number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, what other sources do you think we should look at to determine the number of wounded men from the conflict in July of 1995 in Srebrenica if we wanted to determine that, other than those that I just referenced to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be a very good start. These sources, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Any others that come to mind?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to mind. The Red Cross may have some figures, ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: All right. I agree with you. What about the Bosnian authorities and the insurance programmes that they have for injured veterans or injured military people? Do you think that might help us in determining where they were injured, where they were injured, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Objection on the relevance of this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to respond to that before we decide, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't think it merits a response, with all due response, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, with the respect to category you identified as personal belongings on the corpses, who was in charge of taking that inventory.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pathologist removed the material from the body, took a rough note of it, in general terms, and handed it to the scenes of crimes officers who cleaned them, cleaned the items, and photographed them and logged them carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were there identification papers found on some of the corpse that were recovered?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were in a small number of cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you make an inventory of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in my report. That is -- will be -- there will be an inventory from other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What source would that be?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There will be the scenes of crime documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But you, as the pathologist, did you go over those to determine whether they were accurate and done reliably?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that's not my particular role.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So is there any significance to looking at the personal belongings on the corpses?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as a general observation that we were looking for perhaps things that they didn't have; any bullets or guns, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were you ever provided with a copy of the Prosecution's military consultant and his report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's all the questions I have, Your Honour. Thank you. Thank you, Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. I just want to confirm that Nikolic team, Gvero and Pandurevic teams do not have cross-examination to put.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is correct. We have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there re-examination, Mr. Elderkin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Just on one point, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, on the subject of blast injuries, can you say what kind of weapons blast injuries you came across are consistent with?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commonest or really all of them looked like grenade injuries. And that was on the basis of the material we found, the small portions of metal and little rods, small rods which looked like the contents of a grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. We don't have any further questions for you, Dr. Clark, which means that your testimony ends here. I wish to thank you for having come over to testify again on this trial. You will be escorted, and given all the assistance you need and we wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, we come to documents. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understand that actually everything on the list for Dr. Clark has already been admitted, and we haven't got anything further to tender today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That is our position as well. Defence teams. I start with you, Mr. Ostojic. On page 46, let's go back; let me find back, page 46. When you referred the witness to the War Crimes Pathological Investigation Review, do you intend to tender that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But perhaps you can at least give us an indication of the date when this was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: All I have the date as being 2005. I could get the actual -- I have the article', it's marked. But I would happy, if the Court wants it, you can have it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm asking you in particular because throughout the rest of the transcript, you seem to be referring the witness to page 346, 300, and it seems -- because an article of that length would become a book in itself. So I take it it's the page of the review rather than the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct. It is a journal that has pages, and it's a five or seven-page article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The only reason I didn't submit it because he acknowledged it when confronted with it, so I didn't think -- unless the Court needs it, I would be happy to get a clean copy and submit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I just asked you whether you were tendering because failing that, we needed this clarification. But if you could give indications, please, as to the review itself, the edition, and the precise name of the witness's article.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll provide the Court with that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The title.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have the title now, if the Court would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, if you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There is two. One is entitled, "War Injuries." The other one is titled, "Pathological Evidence." Let me just make sure of that. I'm sorry, "Pathological Investigation." Both appear in the same journal, and they are two or three articles apart from each other. The University of Glasgow, Glasgow, United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't have the issue number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I was surprised it doesn't have the on the actual articles as all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It would have it on the front page of the journal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sometimes they refer with the volume on the pages, but it doesn't. I will provide that the Court, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any of the other Defence teams wishes to tender any documents. None. I think that's it. We can move to the next witness, who is a protected witness, enjoying pseudonym and facial distortion. Yes, Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Dr. Dunjic is still in court. I wonder if it would be suitable for him -- does the Court have a view whether he should remain during the next witness or he should be absent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think this witness is very interesting to Mr. Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: If it is more appropriate for him to be absent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we would leave it entirely in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm sorry I kind of walked up in the middle of Ms. Condon's request, and I guess it concerns the Doctor remaining in the courtroom during the -- my concern is obviously that the witness is a protected witness, and I don't know...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. You are right. Yes. Okay. Dr. Dunjic, I think -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I welcome you to this Tribunal. Madam Usher is going to give you the text of a solemn declaration you are required to make that you will be testifying the truth. Please go ahead. Read it out aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Vanderpuye will be putting some questions to you, and also referring to a statement you made on the 18th of February, 2007. He will be then be followed by some or all of the Defence teams in cross-examination. Before you start testifying, I wanted to confirm to you that we have granted you two protective measures; namely, the use of a pseudonym instead of your real name, and also the use of facial distortion. I just want to make sure that this is to your satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, good morning, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I would like to present the witness with P02445 for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, could you please take a look at that document, and without telling us what's on it, could you confirm that you are the person named in it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. While the Defence is looking at that document, let me first explain to you just a couple of things. I'm going to ask you a series of questions, and I'm going to ask you to try and keep your voice up and allow a small pause between the question and answer to allow the interpreters to do their jobs and make that information available to everyone else. I have only a few questions to ask you, so I anticipate the direct examination will be rather short. First, do you recall having given a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor which was signed and acknowledged on the 18th of February of this year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And the statement that was given by you, is that a truthful statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to read your statement before having come to testify here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you read the statement in your native language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that the language that you originally gave your statement in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And just for the record, can you tell us what language that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Having read your statement, are you satisfied that it is correct and accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does the statement, as you read it, fairly and accurately reflect what it is you actually said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does it fairly and accurately reflect what you would say, if you were to be examined here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does what's contained in the statement accurately reflect what you would say, were you to be examined here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honours, I would offer the statement P02447 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have a very brief summary I would like to read into the record, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like to go into private session just for the first two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. "In 1993, the witness was assigned to the southern site of the Anti-Electronic Warfare Unit, then known as EIPED, and he was assigned there as an intercept operator. Upon his arrival to the southern site, the witness received instructions concerning the operation of the equipment from his commanding officer and began processing intercepted communications in accordance with an established procedure, which entailed taping intercepted communications, manually transcribing them into notebooks, and submitting the handwritten transcriptions for typing and encryption. "The witness remained in the ABiH army until he was demobilised soon after the Dayton Peace Accords took effect." That concludes my 92 ter summary. I have a few questions to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us if you've an opportunity to review a packet of 12 intercepts prior to testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in particular, did you review the handwritten material contained in this packet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does that handwritten material reflect intercepted communications that were taken down by you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you recognise the handwritten material as that of your own?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did you transcribe that material; that is, write the material into a notebook, pursuant to your responsibilities and duties as an operator assigned to the southern site of the Anti-Electronic Warfare Unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to review the original notebooks containing these handwritten intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you satisfied that the copies of these handwritten transcriptions conform -- the handwritten transcriptions contained in the packet conform to the originals that are contained in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions at this time. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic and witness, you both speak the same language, so in order not to create problems for the interpreters that have to translate to us in English and French, please allow a short pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I read your statement, and I saw that you said in the statement that you worked in daily shifts of eight hours each with two operators working at the same time. Can you please confirm that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that you had at that time, at this place where you worked, three sets of equipment. Can you confirm that also?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, since you already mentioned in the statement that you jotted down the conversations into a notebook, can you please tell me when you were in the shift, when you were working, how many notebooks did you have at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I don't remember. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have your own separate notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: When I was in the shift, the notebook was in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And when you finished the shift, did you take it with you or did it stay there for the next person to make entries, the next operator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes. It stayed there and the next operator entered the following entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were working in the shift, did you just have that one notebook, as you said, or did you have several notebooks into which you wrote down different conversations at the same time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Just one notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the notebook was full, you handed it over to a superior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: The superior officer would take the notebook after the conversation was listened back and transcribed into the notebook, if it was urgent; if not, it would stay for an hour, two or three, I don't know for how long, and then the superior officer would do whatever he needed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "after the entry," does that mean that the notebook was taken so that the data could be entered into the computer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: It was my job to transcribe the conversation, to listen back to it, and to write it down. The rest of the work was done by my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the notebook was completely filled, did you again give the notebook to your superior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask you to look at the original notebook where you did make an entry. That is 1268B. Do you see this piece of paper? And I would like to draw your attention to the conversation 255.850. That's the part that I would like you to look at.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me if this is a conversation that you wrote down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I noticed that the entire conversation is written in capitals. Is that how you wrote down all of your conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: We didn't receive any specific instructions about how we should write, so we each wrote how we wished. There was no specific order as to which sort of letters we should use.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't think that there was an order about how you should write, but I'm just asking if it was your habit to write in block letters and if they were always the same size, if that was your habit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because when you look at line 3 of this text, there is a word "pop" there. "Pop left," and so on. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you that because in our language - I'm sorry. I need to slow down a little bit - because in our language "pop" can mean priest, but it can also be a nickname of a person. So I'm asking you this because we cannot really tell from this text what this word refers to. I assume that you didn't know either, you just wrote what you heard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: The word actually is "pop" has been sent, or that has gone to "pop." This happened because the conversations were quite fast, and that's why we wrote quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you didn't understand. I was perhaps unclear. All I'm interested in is this particular word "pop." You wrote down what you heard without indicating specifically, and I assume you didn't know whether this was a profession or a nickname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I didn't know who was being referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I wrote down what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one question relating to this same intercept, this conversation. If you see here, it says in the line below the word -- the line begins, "Parcel, he told you to divide." So can you tell on the basis of this, I cannot see what that word that he told you refers to. So what my question is, is whether you faithfully wrote down what you heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, because this is a little bit -- it's translated a little bit differently, but that is not your problem and I'm not going to bring that to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down. You're moving too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. You mentioned the equipment that you had, and you did specify that in your statement. Can you please tell me if you know whether this was old or new equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know if it was old or new.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one more thing. Do you know which antennas you had? Since I see that you specified the kind of equipment that you had, do you know what kind of antennas you also had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I don't know, but my superiors do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And just one more answer to a question. Do you know if you had your own separate antennas or you had joint antennas -- actually, no, no, I'm sorry that cannot refer to you. I withdraw the question. No, no. Thank you. [In English] [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was just checking the time you have taken. Yes, Defence team for Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. How are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is this the first time you've testified at this Tribunal or any other Tribunal or court concerning your activities in the ABiH army between 1993 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: The first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And if I understand correctly, you met with representatives from the Office of the Prosecutor on the 15th day of February, 2007. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Today is the 20th of February, 2007. And is it correct that you met with Mr. Vanderpuye, the Office of the Prosecutor, and perhaps Dusan Janc, an interviewer, and several interpreters five days ago, here in The Hague. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. When did you meet, if at all, with representatives from the Office of the Prosecutor, including Mr. Vanderpuye, who just questioned you in direct examination?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Could you please clarify the question? When did we meet?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: When did you meet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: You mean the Prosecutor and I?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, yes. Let's start there. That would be fine, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: On the 18th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you don't recall meeting on the 15th day of February?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you meet with any person from the Office of the Prosecutor in connection with your testimony and in preparation for your testimony on the 15th day of February, which would have been last week?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May the witness be shown 65 ter number P2447, which is a witness statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And in -- I don't have the number of the B/C/S but if we could perhaps hand it to the witness. Excuse me, perhaps put it on the ELMO. Do you have it? Could you blow that up, please? Briefly, and I apologise for this, Madam Usher, could you switch back to the English version real quickly, to the last page? And please don't broadcast it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure that the document wasn't being broadcast and accordance with the Court's policy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The other thing is, I don't know if Mr. Meek -- this is an issue that I think can be clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not discuss it at this critical moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear what the witness has to say about this and then you can intervene. Go ahead, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you see on the left of your screen on the bottom, a signature there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is that your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: There are three signatures there. Could you indicate for the record which is yours, the top left, the middle that is a little lower, or the one to the far right, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Top left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, I would ask you to please look to the right-hand side of your screen, that's the document in B/C/S. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And about three quarters of the way down it says, "Date of interviews: 15 and 18.2.2007." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes. This interview was conducted on the telephone on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And who did you speak to over the telephone on the 15th, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I wasn't here on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who -- the question is a simple one. Who did you speak to on the phone on the 15th, or who spoke to you on the 15th on the phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if I may say it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it's -- the question is directed who spoke to you from the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember the name exactly. I know that Snjeska called and told me to prepare myself for the interview, to give a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then you were interviewed over the phone. Was it a male voice that interviewed you or a female voice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Female voice, and I could hear the male voice in the background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you don't know the name of this female who was...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you have the expansion now of the 15th and 18th. I think we can move ahead now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I think I agree with you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: One question, and IF you want to, Witness, tell me if you want to go into private session, but you just stated that you know -- "I know that Snjeska called me and told me to prepare myself." Who is Snjeska? Again, if you need to go into private session to answer that, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I don't know who she is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So can I take it that whoever Snjeska was, was from the Office of the Prosecutor, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I don't know where she's from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And sir, was that the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I apologise. If I may, she said that they need me from the OTP, they need me to give a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Was that the extent of the conversation or did this person, Snjeska, talk to you in more detail about what you -- your statement or testimony was going to be about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, I hate to interrupt you but let's move on. He's told you already that he was then interviewed later but not by this Snjeska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Earlier today, on page 76, you indicated -- or, excuse me, page 74, lines 19 to 20, Mr. Zivanovic asked you some questions, and you indicated that if a conversation were urgent, one of your superiors or a superior would take your notebook immediately and have that conversation then typed. Was that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't do the typing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I understand that. Would it be the supervisor then that would determine if a certain conversation were urgent, ask you to take that notebook so he could type it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So then it's a fair statement that it wasn't you determining what conversations might be urgent, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: We also assessed and informed the superiors. That was our duty. And if a superior was present, that he would monitor our work; and then he would decide whether something was urgent or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, sir, it's my understanding, correct me if I'm wrong, but you would tape record these conversations and then later you would listen to the tape recording and write down what you believed you heard. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And in answer to my colleague's question on page 76 today, you stated that the reason you sometimes wrote, I think, in all bold was because the conversations were quite fast and that's why we had to write quite fast or quite quickly. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I generally write in capital letters; and if there were some mistakes, it was due the haste. Those who the reports were sent to were the ones to decide on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, could you just clarify, if you've already recorded the conversation and you are just listening to it, don't you have the ability to stop the tape and restart it, stop it and restart it, so that you can write it down in a slower fashion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes, we could pause, and then we would rewind, listen to it again, then pause; and then repeat the process until we wrote down everything that was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, but now how do you reconcile that with your answer to Mr. Zivanovic that this happened because the conversations were quite fast and that's why we wrote quite quickly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I said when there was a lot of recorded material then the handwriting was what it was. Sometimes the conversations were slow. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In your statement that you gave to the Prosecutor, under paragraph 3, when you talked about your procedure, you said, "We wrote the channel, date, and time of the conversation and the participants if they had been mentioned during the conversation." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Could you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Referring to the witness statement, which would be 65 ter number P2447, paragraph 3 of your own statement, Witness, when you were discussing how the conversation was recorded to the tape and then listening to the conversation again and writing the conversation in the notebook you said, "The procedure was that we wrote the channel, date, and time of conversation and participants if they had been mentioned during the conversation." Do you remember telling the OTP that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: The date I don't remember, and as for the rest, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, because I didn't notice any dates on any of your handwritten intercepts that you allegedly wrote down. Witness, you also -- or explain this to me: Did you initially tell the Prosecutor's office here that you also signed the transcribed conversation at the end of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Did I tell the Prosecutor? Is that what you're asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in your statement, in your initial statement, maybe on the 15th over the telephone, perhaps? That you would always sign your name at the end.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: At that moment I said that we signed it, although I wasn't sure because it's been a long time. And I wouldn't want to say something that I don't remember and something that I'm not quite sure about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I can appreciate that, Mr. Witness. The tapes that you used were sometimes new and sometimes you were reusing old tapes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, you've got about one minute left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The tapes arrived, my superior placed them, the empty ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So is your answer you always had new tapes or you just know if they were new or you were reusing older tapes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: We didn't use the old tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So it's your testimony --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I apologise. We didn't use old tapes. The ones that already had something recording -- recorded on them, we did not re-record; rather, different tapes arrived. Now, whether they were new ones or had been used before, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Just two more questions. Witness, it's true that when you finished a notebook and it was filled in, it was handed over to your supervisors and you assume that the corps command received them, correct? That was an assumption on your part?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Assumption, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you also had no idea of what happened to the actual tapes after they were finished, other than you believe and assume that they were forwarded to the headquarters. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I don't know where the tapes went afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few questions, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I do not want to go back to the topics covered by my colleagues, but at the southern location, from the first day when you arrived there in 1993, with respect to all of the notes and transcription, you only used the notebooks that were provided to you and you did that all the way until the end of your stay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes, the superior provided the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you ever transcribe intercepts to pieces of paper or small pieces of paper that were later burned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I didn't. Everything went into the notebook; everything that I did went into the notebook. Now, what happened with them afterwards, I don't know. Our superior took them, and I don't know what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So the notebook, the entry into the notebook reflect what you heard on UHER when you recorded a conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And today, if we were to find tapes with these recordings, they would be identical to what is written in the notebook, and you wouldn't enter into the notebook anything that you didn't hear on the tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Nothing else was entered into the notebook except for the conversation that was recorded, at least I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Ms. Nikolic. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a break in about seven minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, in addition to you and your unit at the southern location, this is how we're going to refer to it in the future, there was also another military unit stationed there. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: In addition to us, can you please clarify your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the unit to which you belonged in 1995 at that southern location, was there another unit there who performed other tasks -- which performed other tasks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The way it's been translated at least - and I have no doubt to - I have no reason to doubt that it is a correct translation - would lead the witness to understand that you are asking him whether there were more than one unit in the southern location. While if I understood you correctly, your question was directed to elicit from the witness information as to knowledge of another installation or another location elsewhere and not in the same southern location. Is that correct, Mr. Stojanovic, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. And we have already received answers from witnesses who spoke both about different units performing different tasks and others --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop. I'll just go -- Apart from the southern -- Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Apart from the southern location where you were posted, was there also another location at the north?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you were aware of it then? Don't mention the name. But you were aware of the existence of this other location at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you for assisting me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I would like to ask you this: At the southern location where you were in 1995, was there another facility there not used by your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I know about the facility used by my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I will not be putting any further questions on this topic any longer. Another matter that I wish to ask you about. Was there a service dealing with radio interference or radio jamming within your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I don't know. I worked on intercepting and transcribing and recording intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, at any period during that year, did you or anybody else in your unit maintain communication with the 28th Division in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I didn't. I did the work I described; and what you're saying, I have no idea about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you whether you are familiar with the term "Paket communication"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I heard of that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What does it denote?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: That wasn't my job, so I didn't pay attention to that. I just heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you assist with this, do you know anything about this: In July 1995, an indirect link was established between the 28th Division and the 2nd Corps of the army of BH through the location where you were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And to conclude with this question, how often did you work in eight-hour shifts, as you described earlier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: As a rule we worked in eight-hour shifts, depending on the situation and on operations. Sometimes we worked longer. Eight hours was a rule. Let me clarify. Sometimes there were more than two of us working, and we would also sometimes work longer than eight hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since I will have only just a couple of more questions, we can either stop now or I can go and finish my cross-examination now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long are your couple of more questions, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will stick to what we wrote down, so that's ten minutes in total. So I still have three minutes left, I think, and I will be able to finish within that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's finish with your cross-examination now, and then we have the break in three or four minutes' time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I understood you to say that you worked for eight hours, sometimes longer than eight hours, so what I wanted you to tell me was how many days in a row did your group, you, or your shift work and then after how many days did you get some time off that you were able to spend outside of the location where you worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Well, can I say it like this, can I reply openly to this question, publicly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't see why not. What's your problem with answering it. We are hiding your face. I don't see the problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can answer.
