It's like this: For ten days, we worked at the location - this is my section, the section that I was in - then we were replaced by the second or the other section, which also worked for ten days, meaning that we spent ten days resting, away from the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Looking at the list of the conversations given to us, which you said were yours, they start on the 16th of July, 1995. Would I be correct if I were to say that practically until the 16th of July you were not at the southern location, but that you were away at that time, resting, on leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I am saying what I remember. When I was working, when I was doing that work, I do not recall the dates. Yes, it was a long time ago. I worked and I confirmed that what I wrote down was my handwriting and that I did that work. As for when we were on leave and when would were on duty, that is something that I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. Your Honours, we have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that. We can have the break. 25 minutes starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, in your statement, you said that you marked when you didn't know the name of the person speaking by an X or a Y. I would like to know if it was an established procedure, or it was only the way you would say that it was an unknown correspondent.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes, that was the established procedure when we were not sure who the speakers in the conversation were.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown notebook number 22 with number ERN 0080-4541. Could the page finishing with 4530 be shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, can you see the conversation, the first conversation on this page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Isn't it true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Is it in front of the witness? Yes, okay. All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, can you see the first conversation, is it not true that the participants are noted as 1 and 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that certain of your colleagues did not follow the established procedure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I've told you what I remember; X, Y, question mark. It's possible, but I'm not sure, and that's why I'm saying that I don't remember that they could have been also marked with a 1 and a 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown page, which it has the number 0080-4541.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Seeing the conversation which has been taped at 1355, I would first like to establish is it a conversation which you wrote down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Seeing this page of the notebook, have you any way of establishing the date of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Seeing this conversation on this page of the copy, can you establish the date? Do you have any means to establish the date of this conversation, this intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I don't know. There is no date.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be now shown page which finishes by 4537.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: About the conversation of 9.45, is this an intercept which you wrote down yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that the date which is above has not been written by you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I did not write down the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You don't know who wrote it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you don't know or you don't remember when this date was written down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I didn't write it. I don't remember if we put the dates in or not, and I don't know who wrote the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown page 4514 [as interpreted], four last digits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the problem, usher? I imagine so, but I know when I said it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 4614. It's my fault, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, did you write down the conversation of 9.39? This intercept, did you write it down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you read the first sentence of this intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: "Hey, Krle [Realtime transcript read in error "Colonel"], Milovanovic called me. His Puch has broken down. He has to send it for repairs and says that you should send him transportation until it's fixed."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, it seems that there is a mistake in the translation, anyway in the -- is it true that the first sentence starts by "Krle, Milovanovic?"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Krle. Not Karlo, Krle. K-r-l-e.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So you can see "Krle, Milovanovic" [indiscernible], isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You didn't speak of Colonel Milovanovic in this conversation, did you? Sir, I want to be very specific; it's just for the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Yes. What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: There was a translation problem, and also a transcript problem. I want to discuss it with you. You never mentioned Colonel Milovanovic in this conversation, you just speak of Milovanovic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: I don't recall the conversation, but this is my handwriting. It was a long time ago; I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why don't you be more direct in your question, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would only like to correct an error in translation on page 93, line 10, because indeed it's a mistake in translation or in the transcript. I can't say. But maybe the witness could once again read this sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Witness, can I ask you please to read again that first sentence of that transcript -- of that intercept? Read it aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Hey, Krle, Milovanovic called me. His Puch has broken down. He has to send it for repairs and says that you should send him transportation until it's fixed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that clarifies now the whole -- the whole issue. The problem was translation issue during interpretation. That's all. Your next question, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that during this conversation you only heard one of the speakers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: If two speakers are heard, then it's marked as two speakers in the conversation, and they were heard. X is not known. And Krstic, from practice actually from what we could hear, sometimes they would call him "Krle".

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, I am asking you this question, and answer me only if you know the answer. Do you know who was this Krstic or Krle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Well, I've forgotten who that was. It's been long since then. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the persons you have indicated by X and Krstic, you noted something under Krstic. Could you tell me what is written under the name Krstic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: It's illegible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Give him the notebook itself. Let him look at the notebook. Maybe it's clearer there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's clear to me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And what is written beneath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Not audible." "Inaudible." That means that Krstic is inaudible.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Therefore, indeed, you did hear that only one participant to this conversation was heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: Can you please -- if X, it's one participant that was audible, who could be heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpreter] Could the witness be shown notebook 104 with number 009873. Could the witness be shown page number 2, which finishes by 1873, the digits 1873.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know who is the person you can read the name on this page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you don't know who wrote this name in the notebook, isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And this person did not work with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: The name is not familiar. The first and last name is not familiar.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree that all which is written -- handwritten on this page is indeed a joke?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-153
utterances.text: It's not up to me to speculate on something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I still have one last question to ask, but could we go into closed session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Mr. Josse or Mr. Krgovic, do you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Despite what we'd originally said, Your Honour, we've decided to ask no questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Similar position here, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you just bear with me one moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Witness, that brings your testimony to an end. We don't have any further questions for you. You're free to go. Madam Usher will escort you, and you will receive the assistance you require to return back home at the earliest. On behalf of the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for having come over to give evidence and also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to thank you too, Your Honours, for inviting me here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, let's go through the documents now. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think we -- well, the pseudonym sheet would be -- okay. All right. Everybody has the Prosecution's exhibit to tender. I would submit all of the items that are listed on this tender sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections from the Defence teams? We hear none. So the first two of these documents, that's P02447 being the witness statement, is admitted and to be kept under seal. The pseudonym sheet, P02445, similarly admitted to be kept under seal. All the other intercepts are being entered into the record and marked for identification. The ones which are in bold characters will be kept under seal until we finally decide on the destiny of these intercepts. Any of the Defence teams wishes to tender any document? Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So I think we can close this chapter here. Do you have Professor Wright? In the meantime, for the record, the Defence forensic expert has walked in again into the courtroom. Yes, who will be handling Mr. Wright? Mr. McCloskey -- or Professor Wright. Is he here? So let's bring him in. We can lift the curtains, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll do that, Your Honour. Mr. McCloskey beat me to it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are there interpreters behind that panel or not? Are there interpreters behind that panel? Oh, no. Okay. All right. Because that would make their lives -- I would be jumping. Professor Wright, I welcome you to the Tribunal on behalf of my colleagues. You are about to start giving evidence, of course we will not finish today. Please go through the solemn declaration and we can then start after that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Professor. Please make yourself comfortable. You're familiar with the procedure, as I will pass you on in the very capable hands of the lead counsel for the Prosecution; and then you he will then be followed by the various Defence teams on cross-examination. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor Wright. Can you just begin by telling us your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Richard Vernon Stafford Wright.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's your profession?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I'm an archaeologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As I explained to you, this would be a much shorter process than your memories would have been of the Krstic trial. I won't be asking you very many questions, but I will go over a few things in the next 15 minutes that we have left, just to give a -- for you to give a brief background. Can you tell us, archaeology, what -- can you just briefly describe what that is, especially in the context of the work you were asked to do for the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. In the context of the type of forensic work I was asked to do, the archaeologists are concerned with what's in the ground and the evidence that's associated with bodies in the ground. The anthropologists then study the bones themselves. My role therefore is to find graves, to exhume the graves, and to retain associated evidence and records, and then the bodies are handed over to the morgue for examination by anthropologists and pathologists. Though in the excavations, I have anthropologists with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us why is it that you would have anthropologists with you in the excavations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: They were particularly useful in the graves where there were body parts in -- in determining that a particular collection of bones had no other bones associated with them, and to do that you have to have knowledge of human anatomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there an object to try to remove the -- these bones in some sort of methodical way. I'm sorry, I cannot speak. But what was the purpose of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, the purpose was to recover complete bodies, where the bodies were complete, and the -- to separate out body parts when the bodies were not complete and to send those down to the morgue with separate labels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And aside from as you've described collecting the evidence from the dig, the excavation, did you analyse what you saw and what you worked with sometimes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't analyse the age and sex and cause and manner of death of the individuals, but we certainly analysed the stratification within the graves to see whether they'd been tampered with after primary burial. We had to determine whether the graves were primary graves, that is placed where people had been put after they'd been killed, or secondary graves where they'd been dug up from the primary graves and reburied. So some analysis was required there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Before I'll ask you to give one -- one example of -- of a few graves and how -- what kind of conclusions or analysis you made. But before we get to the actual graves for this case, can you give us a brief background in what kind of experience you had in exhuming mass graves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, at Sidney University, when I had the chair there, I was a general archaeologist and I worked on Australian archaeology; and in 1990, I asked by the Australian government to join a team that went to the Ukraine, and my responsibility there was to find three mass graves that was alleged three Australian people had created, as it were in the Second World War. The first grave was at Serniki and contained 550 bodies, mainly women and children, and my job was to uncover them for the pathologist to examine, in situ in this case. I then resigned from my chair so that I could go back to the Ukraine in 1991, and we discovered and exhumed two more mass graves. I was given the title of emeritus professor and remained not on the payroll as it were of Sidney University since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Those Ukrainian mass graves were Jewish victims killed by the Nazis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I should correct that. They were killed by the Nazis in the case of the Serniki grave; but the other two graves, they were killed by Ukrainians acting on the orders of the German occupiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was your next experience with mass graves after that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: It was in early 1997, I was asked by ICTY to be their chief archaeologist, and I went to the Brcko area in a case that was unrelated to the present one, and we exhumated mass graves there. In the case of what I call the Srebrenica graves, that started in 1998; but in 1999, I reverted to graves that dated from 1992 in the northwest part of Bosnia near Prijedor, and then to Croatia, where we worked on graves where Serbs were victims; and then I came back on to the Srebrenica case at the end of 1999 for Kozluk and in 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you have written reports on your work and you have testified in the Krstic case. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In fact, you've written a reports that postdated your Krstic testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. The excavations at Glogova post date Krstic testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the time small we have, could you just give us an example, and I will use Glogova, since you haven't spoken -- you haven't testified about that. This Court has heard about graves at Glogova, Zeleni Jadar, and they've heard about the Kravica warehouse. Can you just tell us a bit about the -- your exhumations of Glogova and Zeleni Jadar, just briefly to give us an idea of the kind of work and the kind of analysis that -- that you did. And I don't intend for this to be the kind of in-depth that you and I would have done in Krstic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I understand. Yes. My involvement with the sites you have mentioned started at the end of 1998 at Zeleni Jadar 5 in September and October 1998, and we decided that the grave at Zeleni Jadar was a secondary grave; that is, people had been reburied from some earlier place of burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How did you conclude that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: From the fact that many of the bodies were body parts, which is typical of bodies that have been dug up and taken and reburied, bits fall off; then we also found material in the grave that was not -- that it was not possible to link with the area around the grave; for instance, we found motor car parts, hay, those were the main things that struck us. But even the small items like unripe apples were in the grave with the bodies, and it was in the middle of a forest and therefore we interpreted these as exotic objects that had been brought in there with the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And after Zeleni, did you do Glogova at some point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote my report and gave it to ICTY, which included the Zeleni Jadar site in May 1999, in which I predicted some of the properties of the primary grave, but it wasn't until 15, 16 months later; that is, towards the ends of 2000, that I was asked to investigate a site that was called Glogova 1. And when we went to the site, we could see that this had indeed got bits of broken barbed wire of the sort that we'd found in the grave, apple trees. And when we started excavating, it was in a primary grave from which bodies had been taken away. We found with the bodies that had been left in places, motor car parts; hay; and pieces of cement, some broken pieces of cement, some coloured purple, some were cream coloured; bits of plastic foam; and door-frames; and a large joist of the sort that go above doors. These were various parts; and when we put them altogether, they created something which was visible to me when I went down to the Kravica warehouse as having gone missing from there but repairs had been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How did you happen to go to the Kravica because?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I was taken to the Kravica warehouse by ICTY investigators, but -- and I can -- I formed an opinion that the -- that these pieces of building material could be seen at the Kravica warehouse, including the foam insulation, pieces of broken cement had been broken off the Kravica warehouse. But a scene of crime officer, Mr. Mike Hedley, was assigned to write a report on the Kravica warehouse. But I had no doubt when I was carrying out the excavations and when I looked at the Kravica warehouse, that the graves in Glogova were of people who had somehow or rather got mixed up with material from the warehouse. So the sequence in my mind then was that bodies had been taken from the warehouse, incorporated some of the material from the warehouse, buried at Glogova, dug up and taken to -- at least some of them taken to the site at Zeleni Jadar that we had excavated about 15 months earlier, two years earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You had made a brief conclusion that Glogova was a primary grave. Can you give us a bit more detail on how it was that you concluded from your work that Glogova was a primary grave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. There were areas of the Glogova grave site, I'll call it, general grave area, where the bodies were complete; and then there were places where some machine had dug into that pile of bodies. And there was a hole that had been refilled but the hole contained body parts, the refill contained body parts, not complete bodies. And there were the marks of the machine, the tooth marks of a machine on the bottom of what we called these robbing areas. So there were patches of complete bodies that the people had missed, and they were the areas which had been from which bodies had been taken away, new holes had been -- new holes had been dug, but they had -- did not contain complete bodies, they contained body parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I know that this is something we normally would have explained with photographs of the dig and all, but how is that you can tell that there is a hole has been dug and that there's marks in the ground and these things that you are concluding, just by digging?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, it's not just by digging. It's by creating sections in the soil so that you can see the original hole of the primary grave, and then you can then see in the section another hole that's been cut into the previous hole. That's fundamentally a stratigraphic observation that archaeologists make to see where holes have been dug.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any doubt in -- about Glogova regarding your conclusions that you put forward in your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think at this point, Mr. President, Your Honours, we're ready to turn Mr. -- Professor Wright over to the Defence and of course we rely on his reports and his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can safely adjourn now, there is no point in starting a cross-examination with one or two questions and then postponing it all until tomorrow. So Professor, we will see you again tomorrow morning at 9.00. And we will continue with your testimony and I suppose you will be present too. Thank you, and good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 21st day of February, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.,
